# Fashion Design Guide

Status: Canonical design identity  
Theme role: Editorial campaign commerce  
Scope: Documentation only

## 1. Brand Personality

Fashion is for merchants who sell taste, identity, drops, and seasonal desire. It fits apparel, accessories, beauty campaigns, style edits, and brands that need their storefront to feel like a visual magazine with a buy path.

The voice is confident, expressive, image-led, and a little theatrical. It should feel curated and current, not generic retail.

Customers should expect discovery, mood, trend, and collection storytelling. The target emotion is desire: "I want to be part of this look."

## 2. Target Industries

Best fit:

- Fashion
- Accessories
- Beauty
- Footwear
- Streetwear
- Occasionwear
- Influencer-led collections
- Seasonal drops

Acceptable fit:

- Jewelry with editorial photography
- Lifestyle goods
- Premium cosmetics

Poor fit:

- Dense electronics catalogs
- Commodity grocery
- Very quiet design objects

## 3. Design Philosophy

Fashion is editorial first, transactional second, but the path to purchase must remain clear. The theme should use visual drama to create desire and structure to convert it.

Core principles:

- Lead with images, not interface chrome.
- Use strong section rhythm and scale contrast.
- Treat collections as stories.
- Let product cards feel styled, not merely listed.
- Use promotions as campaign moments.

Density changes by section. Heroes and editorials are spacious and dramatic; product grids are cleaner and more disciplined.

## 4. Typography

Font personality: expressive display for campaign moments, paired with a crisp sans-serif for commerce details.

Heading philosophy: large, editorial, high contrast in scale. Headlines may be short, stylized, and confident.

Body philosophy: brief and mood-setting. Avoid long paragraphs.

Price emphasis: prices should be visible but secondary to product image and title. Sale prices may be more expressive during campaigns.

Button typography: uppercase or high-confidence short verbs. Tracking may be used carefully for fashion authority.

Product title hierarchy: product name should feel styled and editorial; collection, fit, color, or drop metadata may support it.

## 5. Color Philosophy

Fashion may use stronger contrast and more expressive accent behavior than Modern, but it should still be curated.

Energy: high.  
Warmth: flexible.  
Luxury: medium to high depending on merchant.  
Neutrality: medium.

Use color to create campaign energy, seasonal emphasis, and visual contrast. Avoid default rainbow merchandising. Accent choices should feel intentional, current, and tied to collection mood.

## 6. Shapes

Shapes may be sharper and more editorial than Modern. Radius should be purposeful rather than friendly by default.

Cards: image-forward, often borderless or lightly framed.  
Buttons: strong rectangles, slim outlines, or high-fashion filled blocks.  
Inputs: clean and fashion-neutral.  
Containers: avoid heavy card nesting; use full-width editorial bands.  
Image frames: dramatic crops, tall portraits, split editorial frames.  
Badges: bold, placed like styling labels or campaign markers.

## 7. Shadows & Elevation

Fashion should not feel like a dashboard. Elevation is secondary to imagery, scale, and contrast.

Use minimal card shadow. Overlays, menus, and drawers can have clean elevation. Hover states may use image zoom, overlay reveal, or text movement rather than heavy lift.

## 8. Spacing Philosophy

Spacing is editorial. It alternates between dramatic open space and tight campaign composition.

Hero and lookbook sections should breathe. Product grids should use enough spacing to keep imagery attractive. Promotional strips can be tighter and rhythmic.

## 9. Product Presentation

Products should feel styled. Image size is important, especially portrait or model-led imagery. Product cards may emphasize image first, product title second, price third.

Fashion favors:

- Tall image ratios.
- Campaign image crops.
- Quick product recognition.
- Optional hover reveal for alternate image or action.
- Strong sale or drop labels when commercially relevant.

The product grid should feel like browsing a collection, not scanning a warehouse list.

## 10. CTA Philosophy

CTAs are confident and campaign-led. Primary CTAs should feel like invitations into a collection: shop the edit, discover the drop, view the look.

Product CTAs may be visible on hover if desktop discoverability is strong and mobile keeps actions accessible. Placement can be more expressive than Modern, but never obscure checkout flow.

## 11. Badge Philosophy

Badges can be bold. They are part of the campaign language.

Sale: strong and visible.  
New: important, especially drops.  
Out of Stock: clear but not ugly.  
Featured: editorial label.  
Discount: bold when campaign-driven.  
Limited: high urgency and desirable.

Badges may overlay images, but placement must preserve the product and model.

## 12. Motion Philosophy

Motion can be elegant and dynamic. Fashion benefits from image reveals, slight zooms, carousel rhythm, marquee-like campaign strips, and smooth section entrances.

Motion should feel controlled and stylish. Avoid playful bounce unless the brand is explicitly youth-oriented. Avoid slow cinematic effects that delay shopping.

## 13. Imagery

Fashion imagery should be large, cropped with intention, and often human or lifestyle-led. Portrait ratios are important. Product-only images should still feel styled through lighting, composition, and background.

Cropping may be dramatic, but never confuse what is being sold. Background treatment may be seasonal, studio, runway, street, or editorial.

## 14. Section Hierarchy

Hero: dramatic campaign statement with large imagery and confident CTA.  
Categories: visual tiles organized by style, gender, season, or collection.  
Collections: editorial story blocks, lookbook grids, or featured edits.  
Featured: image-forward product rows.  
Promotions: campaign moments, strips, or bold banners.  
Testimonials: social proof through creator/customer style snippets.  
Footer: editorial but usable, with clear navigation.

## 15. Customer Journey

The customer arrives through mood and aspiration, enters a collection story, discovers products in context, compares fit/style/price, and checks out while still feeling the brand energy. The emotional curve should be: attraction, imagination, identification, urgency, purchase.

## 16. Do / Don't

Do:

- Lead with editorial imagery.
- Use dramatic typographic scale.
- Make collections feel like stories.
- Use hover imagery and motion with polish.
- Keep the buy path visible beneath the drama.

Don't:

- Make every block a standard ecommerce card.
- Use generic stock-like imagery.
- Hide pricing for the sake of style.
- Let motion slow product discovery.
- Collapse into Pearl by becoming too ceremonial and quiet.

## Certification

Fashion is complete when screenshots feel campaign-led, image-rich, and emotionally expressive, while still preserving a clear ecommerce path.
